1	---
2	name: extract-from-activity
3	description: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from repo activity
7	
8	The **artifact** half of lesson extraction: mine what a window of work left behind — commits, the PRs
9	merged in it, the issue discussion around them — for durable, reusable lessons, and fold each into the
10	repo's **own local packs**. Its sibling [extract-from-conversations](../extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
11	mines the *dialogue*; this one never sees a conversation, only what the work committed.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives are shared with that sibling and stay canonical in
15	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't re-derive it. What follows is only
16	what reading *artifacts* adds.
17	
18	## Capture at the repo's own level
19	
20	Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or
21	mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear. Don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson
22	to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the
23	growth lifecycle's **promote** stage, done canon-side later over whatever merged here; here, just capture
24	it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.
25	
26	## Read the window — and read merged PRs properly
27	
28	Work only the window you were handed (a scheduled run gets it as binding scope in the dispatch issue's
29	Context; an owner's ask names it in words). Never widen it.
30	
31	1. **The commits** — full bodies, and the diff wherever a fix is non-obvious.
32	2. **The PRs merged in the window** — read these *first* and read them *whole*: the diff **and** the
33	   review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source, because it records what
34	   was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won. A verdict reached in review
35	   is a lesson already argued; the commit alone shows only the winner.
36	3. **The issue activity** it names — the comments changed on those numbers.
37	
38	## What artifacts signal — and what they don't
39	
40	The signals worth converting here are the ones an artifact can carry: a fix whose diff is small but whose
41	*reason* is not obvious from the code; a review comment that names a convention the author missed; a
42	revert or a follow-up fix that says the first shape was wrong; a PR that grew several rounds because its
43	approach was re-decided mid-flight.
44	
45	**An already-settled, already-enforced implementation choice is not a lesson.** If a check or a test
46	already pins the shape — which roots a CI sweep walks, which contract a construction must satisfy — and
47	all that is left to say is *why it looks like that*, that explanation belongs as a comment at the
48	implementation site, not as prose in a pack. A rule earns its place by steering a **future** decision or
49	catching a **repeatable** mistake, not by narrating a past one that is already locked in.
50	
51	Wall-time and dialogue friction (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a wait sat through) leave no trace
52	in a diff. Don't infer them from artifacts — that is the conversation sibling's territory, working from
53	logs that actually carry the timestamps.
54	
55	## Landing it
56	
57	Route each keeper down the ladder in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — check first,
58	then pack skill, prose last — into the local pack whose territory owns it. Write more checks and less
59	prose, and keep each addition terse and in the repo's own voice.
60	
61	A new check ships **green or not at all**: see it fail on a violating fixture and pass on a clean one. A
62	rule that cannot be made confident lands as prose instead — never as a broken check.
63	
64	Finding nothing is a perfectly good and common outcome; a duplicate or invented "lesson" is worse than
65	adding nothing.
66

1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first
94	
95	A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
96	retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
97	formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
98	landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.
99	
100	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
101	
102	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
103	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
104	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
105	
106	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
107	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
108	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
109	
110	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
111	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
112	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
113	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
114	silence it replaced.
115

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
29	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
30	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
31	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
32	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
33	
34	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
35	
36	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
37	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
38	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
39	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
40	
41	1. **A check** in that pack's rules — author the `.mjs`, list it on the pack's `pack.mjs`, ship it with a
42	   red-first fixture. Its failure message *is* the lesson.
43	2. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
44	3. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — only what neither of the above can carry.
45	
46	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
47	relocates it. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson warrants segregation, a new local pack is a
48	self-contained directory drop.
49	
50	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all.** A trap from misusing a specific API, class, or
51	library goes as a **comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where the next editor of
52	that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list. Co-locate it in a file's own header
53	comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a
54	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
55	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
56	
57	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
58	
59	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
60	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
61	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
62	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
63

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
11	
12	Your task's declared `expected_outcome` is a **ceiling, not a plan**:
13	
14	- **`open-pr`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
15	  applies to you.
16	- **`merged-pr`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
17	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
18	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
19	
20	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
21	
22	`.claudinite-checks.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
23	
24	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
25	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
26	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading `merged-pr`
27	  to open-pr is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
28	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
29	  materializing it is baselining's converge job, not yours.
30	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
31	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
32	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the dispatch issue.
33	
34	## 2. Arm auto-merge
35	
36	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
37	it once this repo's required checks pass.
38	
39	## 3. When the arm is rejected
40	
41	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
42	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
43	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
44	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
45	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
46	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
47	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
48	  PR's **head sha**:
49	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
50	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
51	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
52	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
53	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
54	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
55	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
56	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
57	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
58	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
59	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
60	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
61	    unseen check does not survive anything.
62	
63	## Never
64	
65	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
66	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
67	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
68	are always legal outcomes.

1	# Shouts & Whispers — the cross-tier delivery contract
2	
3	This project's own pack: the invariants that live *between* the Flutter client and the
4	Cloud Functions, where neither tier's compiler, analyzer, or test suite can see them. The
5	platform packs already own their own halves (`flutter`, `firebase`, `node`), and
6	`spec-driven-product` / `executable-requirements` own the loop and the spec harness — what
7	is left, and what is here, is the handful of agreements that break silently: no error, no
8	red test, just messages delivered to nobody.
9	
10	The product contract these serve is [docs/DESIGN.md](../../../../docs/DESIGN.md) §1; this
11	file is how to keep from breaking it by accident.
12	
13	## Delivery decides the audience once, and it decides it twice over
14	
15	- **A geohash bounds query is a candidate query, never an answer.** `geohashQueryBounds`
16	  returns cells that *cover* the circle, so false positives outside the radius are
17	  guaranteed, not incidental. Every candidate must survive `selectRecipients` in
18	  `firebase/functions/src/recipients.ts` — haversine distance ≤ radius **and** fresh —
19	  before it becomes a recipient. Any future change that widens, caches, or short-circuits
20	  the query keeps the post-filter, or the radius stops meaning anything.
21	- **The sender is a recipient unconditionally.** `selectRecipients` seeds the list with the
22	  sender (`distanceM: 0`, `isOwn: true`) before it looks at a single candidate — the
23	  sender's own copy does not depend on their presence doc existing or being fresh
24	  (DESIGN.md §1.5). `recipientCount` is therefore `recipients.length - 1`, and the two
25	  facts move together: change one and the count reported to the sender starts lying.
26	- **A stale heartbeat means absent, with no fallback.** `PRESENCE_TTL_MS` is the entire
27	  definition of "known to be near" (DESIGN.md §1.2). A user whose last position is older
28	  than the cutoff is not a recipient — never "their last known position, probably still
29	  right". This is the mechanism behind the documented foreground-only limitation
30	  (DESIGN.md §7), so a fix belongs in how presence is *reported*, not in loosening the
31	  cutoff at selection time.
32	
33	## Two encoders, one contract
34	
35	The client encodes presence geohashes with a hand-rolled encoder
36	(`app/lib/geo/geohash.dart`, ~30 lines, no dependency); the server encodes and range-queries
37	with `geofire-common`. They must produce **identical** strings, including at bisection
38	midpoints — both use a strict `>` comparison, which puts a coordinate exactly on a midpoint
39	in the lower half-cell. Touching either encoder means re-running both known-vector suites
40	(`app/test/geohash_test.dart`, `firebase/functions/test/geohash-compat.test.ts`).
41	
42	The matching *precision* is mechanical and is checked (`geohash-precision-parity`), as is
43	the *pairing of the vectors* the two suites carry (`geohash-vector-parity`); the matching
44	*encoding* is not — no scan can run one encoder against the other, which is the whole
45	reason the suites exist — and that is why it is stated here.
46	
47	## One table, two copies
48	
49	[docs/DESIGN.md](../../../../docs/DESIGN.md) §10 is the source of truth for every constant
50	both tiers carry; `firebase/functions/src/constants.ts` and `app/lib/config.dart` are
51	transcriptions of it, kept honest by the `cross-tier-constants` check. Adding a cross-tier
52	constant is a four-part change: the §10 row, the server copy, the client copy, and the
53	`PAIRS` map in the check — a value absent from `PAIRS` is a value nothing is guarding. A
54	constant only one tier needs (the send cooldown, the heartbeat cadence) stays out of `PAIRS`
55	on purpose: it cannot drift, because there is nothing to drift from.
56	
57	## What earns a check here
58	
59	A check in this pack reconciles two committed transcriptions of **one datum** — a constant,
60	a precision literal, a vector table — and dictates no value, shape, or behaviour. Its
61	finding reads *"make the copies agree"*, never *"restore this behaviour"*. A candidate whose
62	finding would command product behaviour is a feature test in disguise: the tier's own suite
63	owns it (`firebase/functions/test/recipients.test.ts`, `app/test/`), and the rule stays
64	prose here.
65	
66	The sender-seed / `recipientCount` rule above is the settled case, and it is **not
67	convertible**: any check for it enforces the seat's existence and its `isOwn` / `distanceM`
68	marking rather than parity between two copies of one datum. It has been converted and
69	rejected twice (PRs #32, #45). It stays prose — do not re-attempt it.
70	
71	Both rejections came from independent re-derivation, not from ignoring a known verdict:
72	each run picked the same rule, built it out, and only then read the prior-run comments on
73	the `Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks` issue. Read those comments *before* authoring a
74	conversion; a rejection recorded there is settled, whatever a fresh reading of the prose
75	suggests.
76	
77	## Running the pack's checks

81	```

=== README ===
# shouts-and-whispers pack (local)

This repo's own pack: the **cross-tier delivery contract** between the Flutter client
(`app/`) and the Cloud Functions (`firebase/functions/`) — the agreements neither tier's
compiler, analyzer, or test suite can see, and that fail silently when broken (no error, no
red test, just messages delivered to nobody).

Declared by hand as `local/shouts-and-whispers` in `.claudinite-checks.json`; never
fingerprinted (`detect`/`marker` are null). It deliberately holds nothing the canon already
homes: `flutter`, `firebase`, `node`, `android`, `ios` own their platforms,
`spec-driven-product` and `executable-requirements` own the loop and the spec harness.

## Checks

| Rule (≤5 words) | Severity | What |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-tier constants agree | blocking | the constants both tiers carry hold the same value, and match `docs/DESIGN.md` §10 |
| Every cross-tier constant guarded | blocking | a constant declared on both tiers is listed in `cross-tier-constants`' `PAIRS` map, so something is comparing the copies |
| Geohash precision matches | blocking | client heartbeat and `sendMessage` encode presence geohashes at the same precision |
| Geohash vectors stay paired | blocking | the two tiers' known-vector suites carry the same precision-9 vectors, with the same expectations |

All four carry a staleness guard: if a guarded declaration or call site is renamed or moved out
of the scanned tree, the check says so instead of quietly passing.

`cross-tier-constants` is deliberately *not* the canon `shared-constants` guard: that one
byte-counts a declared literal per file, which here collides on substrings (`150` inside
`1500`), cannot express the paired identifiers (`WHISPER_RADIUS_M` / `whisperRadiusM`), and
only covers values someone remembered to declare. Pairing by name needs no per-value upkeep.

## Prose (`RULES.md`) — by section

| Section (≤5 words) | How enforced |
|---|---|
| Delivery decides the audience twice | prose (candidate query + post-filter, sender always included, stale means absent) |
| Two encoders, one contract | prose (the encoders' agreement itself) + the `geohash-precision-parity` and `geohash-vector-parity` checks |
| One table, two copies | prose (the §10 row, and why a single-tier constant stays out of `PAIRS`) + the `cross-tier-constants` and `cross-tier-constant-coverage` checks |
| What earns a check here | prose (the pack's own scope bar: reconcile copies, never dictate behaviour) |

## Fixtures

```sh
node --test .claudinite/local/packs/shouts-and-whispers/pack.test.mjs
```

Twenty-four cases: each check red on a violating fixture, quiet on a clean one, red on its
staleness case, and quiet when run against the real repo tree (so a check that stops
matching the project's actual files fails here instead of passing vacuously).

Distilled from this repo's own code and design: `docs/DESIGN.md` §1/§3/§10,
`firebase/functions/src/{constants,index,recipients}.ts`, `app/lib/{config,geo/geohash}.dart`,
`app/lib/adapters/geolocator_location_adapter.dart`, and the paired known-vector suites
`app/test/geohash_test.dart` / `firebase/functions/test/geohash-compat.test.ts`.

{"number":99,"title":"Get the app running on Appetize.io (browser-based device preview)","body":"## Goal

Make the Flutter client in `app/` runnable in the browser via [Appetize.io](https://appetize.io/), so anyone can launch and interact with it on a simulated device without a local Flutter toolchain, a Firebase CLI, or a device. A shareable live demo link alongside the existing golden gallery in `dev/requirements/`.

Moved here from missingbulb/HelloWorldFlutterApp#1, which raised the same idea against a repo that has no native platform projects at all. This repo is the better home: `app/android/` and `app/ios/` already exist, so the original blocker there doesn't apply here.

## What stands in the way here instead

Appetize runs **native builds** — an Android `.apk`/`.aab` or an iOS simulator `.app`/`.zip`. Producing one for this app is not just `flutter build apk`, because the client is Firebase-backed:

1. **`lib/firebase_options.dart` is a committed placeholder that throws** until someone runs `flutterfire configure` (README, "Firebase setup"). An APK built as-is would crash on launch. The build needs real dev-project config (`google-services.json` + generated options).
2. **Google sign-in needs the signing key's SHA-1 registered** in the Firebase console. Whatever keystore CI signs the Appetize build with — debug or a dedicated demo key — its fingerprint must be added, or auth fails inside the preview.
3. **The app is location-first.** It wants a GPS fix before you can send, and reports presence heartbeats while foregrounded. Appetize sessions can inject a mocked location, but a demo where a single visitor is alone in a geohash cell shows an empty feed — the preview needs either seeded nearby presence/messages in the dev project, or a scripted location so visitors land where there's traffic.

## Proposed work

1. **Decide the backend the demo talks to** — the existing dev project, or a separate throwaway `shouts-whispers-demo`. Anything a browser visitor sends lands in real Firestore, so this should not be a project anyone depends on.
2. **Build the artifact** — `cd app && flutter build apk --debug` (Android first; no Apple signing needed). Do it in CI, not a sandbox, so the Firebase config can come from secrets rather than being committed.
3. **Upload to Appetize** — create an account, get an API token:
   ```bash
   curl https://api.appetize.io/v1/apps \
     -F "file=@app/build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-debug.apk" \
     -F "platform=android" \
     -H "X-API-KEY: $APPETIZE_API_TOKEN"
   ```
   Capture the returned `publicKey` / public URL.
4. **Seed the demo** so a first-time visitor sees something: a handful of shouts/whispers near the preview's default coordinates, plus the matching Appetize launch params for that location.
5. **Automate (optional)** — a GitHub Actions workflow that rebuilds and re-uploads on push to the default branch. `APPETIZE_API_TOKEN` and the Firebase config files as repository secrets, never committed.
6. **Document** — an "Appetize.io preview" section in `README.md` with the link, which backend it points at, and how the upload works.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An installable Android artifact builds from `app/` with working Firebase config.
- [ ] The app is uploaded to Appetize and reachable at a public URL.
- [ ] A visitor can sign in, see a non-empty feed, and send a shout/whisper in the browser preview.
- [ ] The demo backend is a project we're content to have strangers write to.
- [ ] The demo link is documented in `README.md`.
- [ ] (Optional) CI keeps the Appetize build current.

## Open questions

- Android only, or iOS too? (iOS needs a simulator `.app` build — more involved.)
- Dev project, or a separate demo project? Who owns the Appetize account and where does `APPETIZE_API_TOKEN` live?

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.
